meta.blurb: Rosa's restaurant has five dishes on the menu, and she cooks every one with care. Lena's life has no menu. She says yes to everything and she is worn out. Rosa shows her how to choose and say no kindly.
meta.bible: Lena: a project coordinator in her thirties who says yes to every request; generous, tired and overloaded. Rosa: a retired chef who runs a tiny restaurant called Little Spoon, calm and wise, whose menu has only five dishes. Daniel: Lena's manager, busy but fair. Mira: Lena's younger sister. Little Spoon: Rosa's small restaurant. Key terms: Priority, Trade-off (what you give up when you choose something), Margin (empty space left in a plan), Boundary, Review. A week has 168 hours and an ordinary year has 8,760 hours. Sunk cost: the idea that we keep going with something only because we have already spent time or money on it. No studies, numbers or quotes are invented. Voice and tone: warm, clear, practical and gently humorous; never harsh about busy people. Added for the full-length book: Brightway: the small events company in Harbour Street where Lena and Daniel work. Tom: a cheerful colleague who is always asking for favours. Priya: a younger colleague, keen to learn, who later takes over some of Lena's tasks. Jo: Lena's old friend, who loves parties. Hana: a friendly neighbour who collects volunteers for the street fundraiser. Omar: Lena's elderly neighbour, who lives on the second floor of Alder Road; his grandson Sami loves boats. Alder Road: where Lena lives. Customer Day: the big event that Lena leads for Brightway in the spring, with about three hundred guests. Little Spoon's five dishes: lentil soup, fresh bread, chicken stew, mushroom rice and apple cake; it has six tables and is closed on Sundays and Mondays. Rosa once worked in a big hotel kitchen with ninety dishes on the menu. Lena's card: a small card with her three priorities, health, Mira and good work. Lena once wanted to join a pottery class. Rosa's three answers: yes, no, and let me think. Lena's no has three steps: thank, say no, stop. The three-hour soup: Rosa cooks her soup for three hours. The word priority was a singular word in English for hundreds of years and meant the one thing that comes first. Seasons: the story runs through about one year, from one autumn to the next.

B1B2: Lena has never really learned how to say no, not even to strangers. She helps with every project, joins every committee and answers every message, and by Friday she is completely worn out.
Before she has even taken off her coat, Tom wants slides, Priya wants advice and Daniel wants a report. Lena smiles and says yes to every one of them.
At lunch, Jo invites Lena to her birthday dinner on Thursday. Lena says yes at once, although she has already promised that evening to someone else.
Lena goes to the leaving party first and stays for twenty minutes. Then she hurries across town to Jo's dinner, where she arrives late and cannot stop checking her phone.
Back at home, Lena sits up in bed and answers messages until midnight. Every reply is polite and quick, but each one adds another small promise.
On Saturday, Mira phones and asks Lena to come to lunch on Sunday. Lena says she would love to, and she forgets that she has just agreed to help a colleague move house.
On Sunday, Lena chooses the move, because she gave that promise first, and she sends Mira a short apology. Mira writes back that it is fine, but Lena can tell that it is not.
On Monday evening, Lena tries to list what she achieved last week. She was busy every hour, yet she cannot name one thing that really mattered.
Lena opens her diary and looks at the coming month. Every day is full of other people's needs, and she cannot find a single hour that belongs to her.
On the way home that evening, it starts to rain. Lena notices a tiny restaurant on Harbour Street with a warm yellow window and a wooden sign that reads Little Spoon.
Lena pushes open the door and steps out of the rain. The room has only six tables, a long wooden counter and a chalkboard on the wall.
A grey-haired woman behind the counter greets her and says her name is Rosa. On the chalkboard Lena reads five dishes: lentil soup, fresh bread, chicken stew, mushroom rice and apple cake.
Lena tells Rosa, a little rudely, that most restaurants have a much longer menu. Rosa laughs and says that she knows, and that this is exactly why she likes hers.
Rosa puts a bowl of soup in front of Lena. She explains that with only five dishes, she can give each one all of her attention.
Lena tastes the soup and stops talking at once. It is rich, sweet and peppery, and for the first time in weeks she is eating slowly.
Rosa shows Lena an old photograph of a huge, shining kitchen. She used to be head chef in a hotel, she says, where the menu had ninety dishes.
Rosa remembers that the hotel guests were always happy. Yet she knew the food was never as good as she wanted, because there was never enough time to get it right.
A man at the door asks if she could make a pizza for his children. Rosa tells him warmly that she cannot, and she suggests a good pizza place that she knows down the road.
A regular customer pays and says that he will be back on Friday for the stew. Rosa explains that people love Little Spoon because they always know what they will find.
When Lena finally stands up to leave, she asks if she can come again. Rosa writes Tuesday on a napkin and tells her to bring her diary and her appetite.
Lena arrives on Tuesday with her diary, as Rosa asked. Rosa pushes aside the bread basket and lays a big blank planner on the counter, with seven columns and twenty-four rows.
Rosa asks Lena how many hours a week contains. Lena multiplies seven by twenty-four, writes 168 at the top of the page and feels surprised by how small the number looks.
Rosa asks Lena to colour in her sleep first. If she sleeps eight hours a night, that is 56 hours, so only 112 hours are left for everything else.
Lena colours her work, her journeys and her chores. Work takes about 45 hours, travel about 8 and meals and chores about 25, so only about 34 hours remain.
Rosa writes 8,760 on a napkin and tells Lena that this is the number of hours in an ordinary year. They will pass, she says, whether or not Lena chooses how to spend them.
Lena suddenly realises that nobody in the world can buy any extra hours. A millionaire has exactly the same 168 hours as she does, and nobody can make a longer week.
Rosa takes a sack of flour from the shelf. She says that it can make bread or cakes, but if she uses it all for rolls, she cannot also bake the cake.
Rosa asks Lena to write all of her promises into the planner. Lena writes and writes, and soon the boxes overflow and run off the edge of the paper.
Lena laughs at first, and then she goes quiet. For years she has been promising hours that do not exist, like someone who writes cheques without any money in the bank.
Rosa tells Lena that she is neither lazy nor weak, but only trying to pour a bucket of water into a cup. Then she asks Lena to note every yes that she gives this week.
All week, Lena makes a small mark in her notebook each time she says yes. By Wednesday lunchtime she has twenty-three marks, and she has not even been counting the smallest favours.
Rosa tells Lena that every yes is also a no. If Lena agrees to a new project, she is saying no to the time that she could have spent on something else.
Lena remembers a pottery class that she has wanted to join for two years. It meets on Thursday evenings, which are exactly the evenings when she always stays late at work.
Rosa says that when people buy a coat, the price is written on a tag. When they spend an hour, there is no tag, so they often forget that it costs something.
Rosa says that she has made some difficult trade-offs herself. She closes the restaurant on Sundays and Mondays, which means less money but also a rested mind and a calm kitchen.
Rosa says that a quick favour is rarely quick. You must stop what you were doing, do the favour, and then find your place again afterwards.
On Thursday, Tom asks for help with another presentation. Lena does not say yes at once, and instead she writes down what she would give up: her lunch break and her quiet afternoon.
This time Lena decides that helping Tom is worth the cost, so she says yes and gives him half an hour. It feels completely different, because she has chosen it and nobody has forced her.
Mira comes round on Friday evening and notices that her sister looks calmer. Lena draws two doors on a napkin and tells her about trade-offs, and Mira listens with wide eyes.
That night Lena looks at the photographs on her wall, at friends, colleagues and cousins. She asks herself a simple question: why does she say yes to all of them?
On Tuesday, Rosa asks Lena why she says yes so quickly. Lena looks at her hands and admits that she is afraid of disappointing people.
Lena remembers being a small girl at school who always carried the teacher's books. Everyone praised her for being so helpful, and she loved the warm feeling it gave her.
Over the years, helping became the way that Lena earns love. Deep down, she is afraid that if she stops being useful, people will stop wanting her around.
Rosa listens and then says that being helpful is a beautiful quality. The trouble starts, she says, only when yes is the one answer you are able to give.
Lena admits that she also says yes because she wants to be liked. When she skipped Jo's party once, she spent the whole evening worrying about what people were saying.
Rosa says that the fear of missing out is natural. But nobody can be everywhere, she explains, and every choice leaves a thousand other things behind.
Rosa says that saying yes is the easy thing to do in the moment. The cost arrives next week, she says, and it is paid by a different Lena who never agreed to it.
Lena says that saying no feels like a fight to her. She can already see the other person's disappointed face, and her stomach turns over.
Lena thinks hard for a moment about this strange question. Last month, a colleague told her that she could not help with a task, and Lena forgot all about it before lunch.
Lena takes a napkin and writes four reasons: letting people down, being liked, missing out and having a fight. Seen on paper, they look much smaller than they did inside her head.
Rosa asks what the yeses have cost her so far. Lena thinks about her tight shoulders, her short temper and the way she snaps at people she loves.
One morning Daniel returns a report to her desk with a dozen small red marks on it. Lena knows that she could have done much better if she had not been rushing.
Mira has a little art show at a café on Friday. Lena arrives an hour late with her phone in her hand, and she sees from Mira's face that she has been waiting.
Even when Lena is sitting with friends, she is always checking her messages. Her body is at the table, but her mind is already working on the next task.
At home, Lena sits in the dark living room beside a pile of unfinished work. She is too tired to read, to cook or even to enjoy the quiet.
Rosa tells Lena about a night when the hotel was full and she tried to stir ten pots at once. She burned the sauce, the rice and the fish, and every guest had to wait.
Rosa asks Lena to think about the people who depend on her. When Lena is late or careless, Tom has to wait for her file and Priya cannot finish her own work.
Rosa explains that a yes is a promise, and that broken promises make a yes cheaper. If Lena says yes less often, she says, each yes will be worth much more.
Lena looks hard at herself in the mirror that night. She does not want to be a person with a thin and tired yes, and she decides to change.
When Lena returns to Little Spoon, she tells Rosa that she is ready, and she asks what to do first. Rosa smiles and says that the first step is to choose what she wants to say yes to.
Rosa gives Lena a clean sheet of paper and a pencil. She asks her to write one big question at the top: what do I want this year to be about?
Lena lists the report, the emails and the office party. Rosa reads the page and says that these are chores, and not the things that a year can be about.
Rosa asks Lena to remember a day when she felt truly happy and proud. Lena thinks of a summer afternoon by the sea with Mira, and of a project that she once finished with real pride.
Lena writes fifteen things that matter to her, from travel and cooking to friendship and learning. Rosa smiles and says that if everything is important, then nothing is.
Rosa tells Lena a small and curious fact about the history of words. For hundreds of years the word priority was only singular, because it meant the one thing that comes first.
Lena starts crossing things out, slowly and painfully at first and then faster. After ten minutes only three words remain on the page, and she draws a heart around them.
Rosa says that three is a very good number, and that one or two would be even better. Nobody can hold more than a few priorities at once, she explains, so they are chosen for one season of life.
Lena worries that she is choosing for the rest of her life. Rosa reassures her that these priorities are only for this season, and that she is free to choose differently later.
Rosa asks Lena to say her three priorities aloud. They sound strange at first, almost too simple, but by the third time they sound completely true.
Rosa tells Lena to keep the card in her diary. It is like a menu, she says, because it tells you what you serve, and also what you do not.
On Wednesday morning, Tom asks Lena to join a new committee for the office garden. Lena takes out her little card and looks at the request and the card side by side.
The first question is whether the request fits health, Mira or good work. The garden committee is a pleasant idea, but it fits none of the three.
The second question is the one about the trade-off. The committee would meet every Wednesday afternoon, which is exactly the time Lena uses to write her careful reports.
Even now, Lena can feel the old yes climbing up her throat, like a hiccup that she cannot control. She presses her lips together and takes a slow, deep breath.
Lena begins to understand that the real secret of all this is the pause. Between the question and the answer there is a small space, and she can use it to think.
Lena smiles at Tom and gives him the phrase that Rosa taught her. She says, “Let me check my diary and get back to you.”
Lena goes for a short walk around the block. The cold air clears her head, and she finds that the answer is much easier to see when nobody is waiting for it.
Back at her desk, Lena writes her answer three times. The first is too long and the second is too stiff, but the third is short, honest and kind.
That evening, Rosa tells Lena that there are really three possible answers to a request. They are yes, no, and let me think, and the third is the one that protects the other two.
Lena had expected something dreadful to happen because she made Tom wait, but nothing does. Tom does not even mention the committee again that day, and she sleeps well.
Rosa decides that Lena needs to practise, just like a pianist. She pretends to be a customer who asks for a favour, and Lena has to say no out loud.
Rosa teaches a short formula and taps the counter three times. First thank the person, then say no clearly, and then stop talking.
On her first attempt, Lena explains for two whole minutes and apologises six times. Rosa raises her hand and says that Lena sounds like a lawyer defending herself in court.
Rosa explains that a long explanation is not a kindness. It gives the other person something to argue with, and it makes the no sound like a negotiation.
Lena returns to her desk, takes a deep breath and writes to Tom. She thanks him for the invitation, says that she cannot join the committee, and presses send with a shaking finger.
A minute later, Tom's reply arrives on her screen. He writes that it is no problem and thanks her for letting him know, and Lena stares at it in amazement.
That weekend, Hana from next door asks Lena to join her street fundraiser. Lena thanks her warmly, says that she cannot do it this year, and wishes her good luck.
When a colleague asks for help with a presentation, Lena says no but offers a small alternative. She points him to a good template and tells him that Priya made a similar deck last month.
Rosa warns Lena very firmly not to invent excuses. A made-up reason has to be remembered, and sooner or later it will be found out, but the plain truth never needs defending.
Rosa tells Lena that a good no is aimed at the request and not at the person. She says no to the pizza, but she is still glad to see the man and his children.
Lena has refused Tom and Hana, but her manager is a different matter. Daniel decides her future at Brightway, and the thought of disappointing him makes her feel sick.
Rosa tells Lena not to say no to her manager at all. Instead she should show him the trade-offs and ask him which task he would like her to put first.
Lena spends an evening making a one-page list of every project she has. Beside each one she writes how many hours it will really need, and the total makes her gasp.
On Monday, Lena sits down with Daniel and shows him the page. She says that she can do all of these things, but not all of them well, and she asks which one should wait.
Daniel admits that he had no idea how much work Lena was carrying. He says that he had always assumed she would tell him if it was too much.
Daniel takes a pen and crosses out one task, which he moves to next month. He gives another to Priya, who has just asked for more responsibility.
